strengths: DRE-BO-SSL offers a simple, potentially useful combination of classification-based Bayesian optimization with label propagation and label spreading. Supporting both sampled unlabeled points and existing candidate pools gives the approach a clear practical scope.

The evaluation covers synthetic optimization, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-derived search task. Twenty repetitions with reported standard errors provide meaningful empirical evidence, with particularly promising sample-efficiency gains on NATS-Bench and several synthetic problems.

The appendices investigate bandwidth, unlabeled sample count, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling, including a labeled-only comparison. These studies expose useful sensitivities, and the paper acknowledges computational limitations and the difficulty of transferring existing semi-supervised learning theory to adaptive optimization.
weaknesses: The central claim that unlabeled data alleviates overconfidence and improves exploration is insufficiently isolated. The qualitative Branin examples do not establish that broader high-scoring regions produce better exploration. Figure 11 shows the no-transductive baseline outperforming the proposed variants on Bukin6 and outperforming label spreading on Branin. Moreover, this ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main experiments learn it. Comparisons that control bandwidth and separately ablate propagation and randomized tie handling are needed to distinguish the proposed mechanism from classifier choice and tuning.

The cluster-assumption justification does not follow from the sampling construction. Truncated Gaussians centered on evaluated points need not produce high-density regions with homogeneous objective-threshold labels; uniformly sampled synthetic pools likewise provide no general separation between classes. Appendix C does not establish that propagation expands the desirable decision region or improves optimization, and explicitly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. results do not apply. Consequently, the claims of mitigating overconfidence or obtaining superior classifiers remain heuristic rather than theoretically supported.

Important implementation details are missing despite their direct influence on the comparisons. These include feature scaling and categorical encoding, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, and bandwidth optimization bounds and initialization. It is also unclear how acquisition maximization works over finite candidate pools given the stated use of L-BFGS-B. These omissions are consequential for a method built on Euclidean similarities and make reproduction and assessment of comparison fairness difficult.

The MNIST experiment relies on embeddings trained using 440,000 labeled examples of the same three-digit recognition task that defines the optimization objective. Although the training and search splits are separate, this supplies substantial objective-related supervision and limits the experiment's evidence for label-scarce black-box optimization. A baseline that ranks candidates directly using the pretrained classifier is especially important for establishing whether sequential optimization adds value.

Practical generality is less established than the breadth of benchmark names suggests. Continuous optimization is tested only on four two-dimensional functions, and random search and TPE are absent. The timing study compares pool subset sizes within the proposed method rather than against competing optimizers. Given dense graph computations, repeated bandwidth fitting, and 1,000 acquisition-optimization starts, comparisons of performance against elapsed time would help establish practical value.

A correctable mathematical inconsistency affects the algorithm description: the definition p_ij = w_ij / sum_k w_kj implies P = W D^{-1} for the symmetric similarity matrix, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W and Equation 7 propagates using P transpose. These conventions generally produce different updates and should be reconciled. This is secondary to the evidential concerns above, but matters for faithful implementation.
